title: Which Chart? Think Before You Draw

lines: o1
You've got the data. You've got a deadline. And you've got a menu full of charts.
o2
So which one do you pick?
o3
Most of us pick the one that looks right. Let's rewind.
n1
Tamara Munzner describes design as four nested layers. The domain: who the readers are, and what they care about. The data and task abstraction. The visual encoding. And the algorithm that draws it.
n2
Each layer depends on the one around it. Jump straight to the chart, and you can build something polished that answers the wrong question.
n3
So we'll walk three signposts, in order. What. Why. And how.
w1
First: what is the data? Every row is an item. Here, one day of bike hires. Every column is an attribute.
w2
And every attribute has a type. Day type is categorical: weekday, Saturday, Sunday. There's no order to them.
w3
Try sorting them from smallest to largest, and the labels just shrug.
w4
Month is ordered. And it's time: one moment leads to the next.
w5
Number of hires is quantitative. You can measure it, add it, and say one month had more than another.
w6
N, O, or Q. And is it time?
y1
Second: why is the reader looking? Imagine two readers with the same table.
y2
One asks: which month was busiest? The other: do busier months mean longer rides?
y3
Munzner splits every task into an action and a target. Compare the months, and your target is the extremes. Check whether two measures move together, and your target is a relationship.
y4
Same data. Different job. Different chart. Most jobs you'll meet sit on one of four cards: compare and rank, part of a whole, trend over time, and relationship.
h1
Third, and only now: how should it look? A chart is made of marks, like dots, lines and bars, whose appearance changes to carry the data. Those changes are channels.
h2

People read some channels far more accurately than others. Position along a shared axis is the best we have. Then position on separate axes. Then length. Angle and area sit much lower, and colour lower still.
h3
Munzner's two rules are simple. Be expressive: show what's in the data, and nothing that isn't. Be effective: give your most important attribute the most accurate channel.
p1
Let's test it. Here are TfL's 2024 cycle hires, month by month, drawn twice. The question: which month was busiest?
p2
On the pie, you're comparing angles, and twelve slices look almost the same. On the bar, every length shares a baseline, so you can rank them: July, just ahead of August and June.
p3
One category, one number each. Both charts can show it, so the type doesn't decide. The task does. To compare twelve months, you want length on a common baseline. That's a bar.
p4
Now a different question: what share of the year's hires came on weekdays, Saturdays and Sundays?
p5
Three parts that really do add up to a whole. Here, a pie does its one job well. Three quarters of all hires were on weekdays.
p6
Few parts. A real hundred per cent. Otherwise, bar is your default.
l1
Two numbers on two axes. Line, or scatter? Ask whether your points form a sequence.
l2
Months follow one another, so a line says, honestly: this continues into that. Hires climb through spring, peak in July, and fall away by December.
l3
Now each dot is one month's pair of measures: how many hires, and the average hire time in minutes. The question is whether busier months mean longer rides.
l4
They do. The dots rise together, from about fifteen minutes in winter to nineteen in summer.
l5
Join the dots in month order, and the line runs up, then doubles back over itself. It tells a story about time that this chart was never asking. That's the expressiveness rule at work.
r1
So, before you open the chart menu, walk the path.
r2

One: what are my items, and what are my attributes? Two: what type is each one? N, O, or Q, and is it time? Three: what must the reader do? Choose the chart whose strongest channel, position first, serves that task.
r3
What is it. Why are they looking. And only then, how should it look. Do that, and the chart picks itself.
e1
Your turn. Four new data sets. Which chart, and why?
